question: What cost discount does the Message Batches API offer versus the synchronous API?
options: About 50% off the synchronous price.
About 25% off the synchronous price.
Exactly the same price; the difference is throughput.
Free for the first 24 hours of each month.
explanations: Correct. The Message Batches API is priced at roughly 50% of the synchronous API.
25% understates the discount; the documented figure is ~50%.
Pricing is genuinely lower for batches, not the same.
There is no documented free-window pricing; the discount is a flat ~50%.

question: What is the processing-window guarantee for the Message Batches API?
options: Guaranteed 24-hour delivery exactly.
Up to 24 hours, with no latency SLA.
Guaranteed 1-hour delivery for premium tiers.
Best-effort under 5 minutes.
explanations: There is no exact-24h guarantee; 24h is an upper bound.
Correct. The documented characteristic is 'up to 24 hours' with no SLA — an upper bound, not a guarantee.
No premium tier accelerates batches to 1 hour; the API has no latency SLA.
There is no sub-5-minute target; most batches finish faster than 24h but no SLA applies.

question: Which workload is the canonical good fit for the Message Batches API?
options: An interactive chat assistant for live customer support.
A pre-merge check that gates developer merging.
An overnight technical-debt report read at the morning standup.
A synchronous HTTP API endpoint with a 3-second timeout.
explanations: Live chat is blocking; users won't wait hours for replies.
Pre-merge checks block developers; 'up to 24h, no SLA' is incompatible.
Correct. Overnight reports are the textbook non-blocking, latency-tolerant workload.
A 3-second HTTP timeout cannot tolerate up-to-24h batch processing.

question: Why is the Message Batches API a poor fit for a CI pre-merge security check?
options: Batched requests cost more for code-review workloads.
The Batches API doesn't support security-related prompts.
The Batches API can't accept code as input.
Pre-merge checks block a developer; up-to-24h, no-SLA processing breaks the merge gate.
explanations: Batches are ~50% cheaper, not more expensive.
There's no content restriction on security prompts.
Code is just text input; batches accept it fine.
Correct. Blocking workflows can't tolerate the no-SLA, up-to-24h window.

question: Does the Message Batches API support a multi-turn tool-use loop within a single request?
options: No — multi-turn tool calling requires the synchronous API.
Yes, with up to 4 tool turns per batched request.
Yes, but only for built-in web search.
Yes — batched requests run an internal tool loop transparently.
explanations: Correct. The Batches API does not orchestrate tool loops mid-request; that requires the sync API.
There is no documented N-turn limit because the feature isn't supported.
The limit is not 'web search only'; multi-turn tool-use is unsupported in batch.
There is no transparent internal loop; your code must orchestrate, which requires sync.

question: What is the purpose of the `custom_id` field on a batched request?
options: It's a server-assigned token used for billing reconciliation.
It's a caller-supplied identifier echoed back on the response so you can correlate which result belongs to which input.
It selects which model variant the batch should use.
It encrypts the request payload end-to-end.
explanations: Billing identifiers are separate; `custom_id` is for application-level correlation.
Correct. `custom_id` is set by the caller and returned on the matching response for correlation.
Model selection uses the `model` field, not `custom_id`.
`custom_id` doesn't encrypt anything; transport is TLS.

question: A nightly batch of 50,000 requests has 3 failures (context-length errors). What's the right resubmission strategy?
options: Skip the failures and update the dashboard with partial results, ignoring the 3.
Resubmit the entire batch from scratch.
Identify the 3 failed `custom_id`s, chunk the inputs as needed, and resubmit only those.
Switch to the synchronous API and re-run all 50,000 immediately.
explanations: Silently dropping records is bad data hygiene and the failure mode is fixable.
Wastes a 24-hour cycle and money on the 49,997 already-successful requests.
Correct. Resubmit only the failed `custom_id`s, chunked or fixed; don't waste a 24h cycle on the 49,997 successes.
Re-running 50,000 sync defeats the cost savings and isn't necessary when only 3 failed.

question: An SLA promises customers results within 30 hours of upload. Batches process in up to 24 hours. What submission cadence honours the SLA worst case?
options: Submit only when 10,000 requests have queued.
Submit once a day at the same UTC hour.
Submit every 30 hours, matching the SLA.
Submit every ~4 hours (so worst case is queue + 24h ≈ 28h).
explanations: Volume-triggered submission doesn't bound queue wait; an SLA-driven cadence does.
An item arriving 1 minute after the daily submission waits 24h queued + 24h processing = 48h, breaking the 30h SLA.
30h cadence + 24h processing = 54h worst case, far outside the SLA.
Correct. Worst-case end-to-end = queue wait + 24h processing; with 4h cadence, that's 28h, inside the 30h SLA.

question: A team plans to batch a 200,000-document JSON-extraction job. What should they do *before* submitting the batch?
options: Run a small representative sample synchronously, refine the prompt until first-pass success is high, then batch.
Submit the batch and rely on Anthropic's automatic retries to fix failures.
Skip prompt refinement; the batch processing is deterministic.
Use the synchronous API for the whole job to ensure correctness.
explanations: Correct. Pre-batch refinement on a sample maximises first-pass success and avoids burning a 24-hour cycle on a prompt bug.
Anthropic doesn't auto-fix prompt bugs; failures show up in your response file as your problem.
Prompt quality directly drives first-pass success; skipping refinement risks a 24h re-run.
Sync defeats the 50% savings; the right move is to keep the batch but validate the prompt first.

question: Your manager proposes switching both an overnight tech-debt report and a blocking pre-merge check to the Batches API for 50% cost savings. How should you respond?
options: Switch both; the cost savings outweigh latency concerns.
Switch the overnight report only; keep the pre-merge check synchronous.
Switch both, with a sync fallback if a batch runs over 1 hour.
Switch neither; the Batches API isn't production-ready.
explanations: The pre-merge check blocks a developer; up-to-24h, no-SLA processing makes the merge gate unusable.
Correct. Batch fits the non-blocking overnight report; the blocking pre-merge check must stay sync.
Sync fallback doubles cost (you pay for the abandoned batch slot) and doesn't beat plain sync's worst case.
Batches are production-ready; the issue is matching workload to API.

question: A team is planning a nightly bulk classification run. Which fact about the Message Batches API most directly determines whether it's an appropriate choice?
options: There is no latency SLA; processing can take up to 24 hours.
Batched requests can include up to 100,000 messages each.
Batches are billed on the input token count alone.
Batched responses are returned in submission order.
explanations: Correct. The latency characteristic is the deciding factor — overnight bulk work fits because nothing is waiting.
Throughput limits aren't the architectural fit question; latency tolerance is.
Pricing is on input + output tokens; in any case, billing details don't decide workload fit.
Order is not guaranteed — that's why `custom_id` exists, and it's not the deciding fit factor.

question: An overnight research workflow runs a tool-use loop: Claude calls `web_search`, your code runs it and appends the result, Claude calls `fetch_page`, etc. The team wants 50% savings via batches. What's the correct migration?
options: Move the entire loop into a single batched request — the batch runtime executes tools internally.
Keep the agentic loop on the sync API, or pre-fetch all data deterministically and batch only the final single-turn synthesis.
Wrap each tool call in its own batched request and stitch responses together.
Use batches with a 4-hour timeout to bound loop length.
explanations: Batch runtime does not execute tools mid-request; the loop never advances past turn one.
Correct. Batches don't support multi-turn tool-use; either keep the loop on sync or decompose into pre-fetch + batched synthesis.
One batched request per tool call doesn't reproduce loop semantics — you need the model to see prior tool_results in context.
There is no per-batch tool-loop timeout because the feature isn't supported.

question: A pipeline submits a batch of 200,000 invoices. The response file arrives unordered. How should the pipeline match each response to its source invoice?
options: Match by input prompt prefix; identical prefixes share an output.
Match by index — request N corresponds to response N in the response file.
Set `custom_id` to a stable per-invoice identifier (e.g., the invoice ID) at submission and key the response file by it.
Use a hash of the model's response text to look up the source invoice.
explanations: Prompt prefixes aren't unique correlation keys, especially with shared system prompts or templates.
Response order isn't guaranteed; positional matching silently misaligns results.
Correct. `custom_id` is the documented correlation mechanism — caller-supplied, echoed back on the response.
Hashing response text is post-hoc and unreliable; correlation must be built in at submission time.

question: A vendor processes uploaded contracts in batches with a 30-hour SLA. They currently submit one batch per day at 02:00 UTC. Customers report their results sometimes arrive ~48 hours after upload. What is the fix?
options: Cache responses for 24 hours to mask the latency.
Renegotiate the SLA to 48 hours.
Move every customer to the synchronous API.
Submit batches every 4–6 hours so worst-case `queue_wait + 24h` stays within the 30h SLA.
explanations: Caching responses doesn't help requests that haven't been processed yet.
Renegotiating the SLA is a business workaround, not a technical fix; the math problem is solvable.
Sync defeats the 50% cost savings on a workload that's perfectly suited to batches.
Correct. With a daily cadence, an upload arriving just after 02:00 waits 24h queued + 24h processing = 48h. A 4–6h cadence keeps worst case inside 30h.

question: A team batches 100,000 documents through a JSON-extraction prompt and finds 18% fail schema validation due to an ambiguous instruction. What's the most cost-effective remediation pattern going forward?
options: Refine the prompt on a small synchronous sample until first-pass success is high, then run the full batch.
Always submit two batches in parallel — the second as a backup if the first fails.
Add a sync fallback that re-runs each schema-failed request immediately after the batch.
Lower the temperature to 0 and ignore prompt refinement.
explanations: Correct. Pre-batch refinement on a sample exposes ambiguity in minutes; fixing it post-batch costs another 24h cycle.
Parallel batches double cost without addressing the root cause (the ambiguous prompt).
A sync re-run is a band-aid; refining the prompt eliminates the 18% failure rate at the source.
Temperature 0 doesn't fix instruction ambiguity — it just makes the wrong interpretation deterministic.

question: A developer says: 'I'll batch the nightly job because it's huge — 1M documents.' What's wrong with the reasoning?
options: Nothing — large jobs are exactly when batching is required.
Volume isn't the criterion for batching — latency tolerance is. The right question is whether anyone is waiting on each response.
1M documents exceeds the per-batch maximum, so it can't be batched at all.
The 50% savings vanish above 100k requests.
explanations: Large jobs don't automatically belong on batches; a huge interactive workload still needs sync.
Correct. Volume can make batching attractive, but a small overnight job is also a great fit and a huge real-time job still isn't.
1M documents can be split across batched requests; volume isn't the blocker.
There's no documented step-down in the discount based on volume.

question: A weekly eval run currently uses the synchronous API for ~10,000 requests and finishes in about 20 minutes on Friday afternoons. The team wants to halve the cost. Should they migrate to batches?
options: No — eval runs require multi-turn tool calling, which batches don't support.
No — anything that currently completes in 20 minutes is too latency-sensitive for batches.
Yes — eval runs are non-blocking; submit on Friday morning and tolerate the up-to-24h window for the cost saving.
No — the 50% discount only applies to overnight jobs.
explanations: Eval runs are typically single-turn classifications or scorings; tool-use loops are uncommon.
20 minutes vs 24h doesn't matter if no one is waiting on the result; latency tolerance is the criterion, not current speed.
Correct. Evals are a textbook non-blocking workload; pay half as much in exchange for tolerating the 24h upper bound.
The 50% discount applies generally, not 'overnight only'; the timing fit makes it work for any latency-tolerant workload.

question: Which statement most accurately describes the Batches API's processing latency in production planning?
options: Treat batches as effectively synchronous because they 'usually finish in a few minutes.'
Treat 24h as the expected delivery time and align deadlines accordingly.
Treat 24h as a soft target; Anthropic compensates if it slips.
Treat 24h as a worst-case upper bound; design so deadlines hold even if the batch finishes at hour 23.
explanations: 'Usually finishes fast' is observation, not guarantee; production design must hold at the worst case.
Designing to the upper bound as 'expected' confuses upper bound with mean — fast runs don't mean future ones will match.
There is no SLA, so there's no documented compensation for slippage.
Correct. 24h is an upper bound, not an expected time; plans must hold at the worst case.

question: A team's batch returns 1,200 of 50,000 responses with `isError: true` because those documents exceeded the context limit. The simplest reliable remediation is:
options: Identify the 1,200 by `custom_id`, chunk those documents into smaller pieces, and resubmit only the chunks.
Resubmit the entire 50,000-request batch with a higher `max_tokens`.
Drop the 1,200 documents from the dataset; they're outliers.
Switch to a model with a smaller context window.
explanations: Correct. `custom_id` makes targeted resubmission cheap — chunk the oversized inputs and re-batch only those.
Re-running all 50,000 wastes a 24h cycle and money; the 48,800 already-successful results are unchanged.
Silently dropping data is bad hygiene and the failure mode (context overflow) is fixable by chunking.
Smaller context shrinks capacity, which makes the failure worse, not better.

question: Which workload combination is correctly matched to the Message Batches API?
options: Live customer support chatbot and an overnight tech-debt scan.
Weekly compliance audit over 50k transactions and a nightly classification of 1M documents.
Pre-merge security check and a CI lint job.
Synchronous HTTP endpoint with a 5s timeout and a real-time fraud-detection feed.
explanations: Live chat is blocking; only the overnight scan fits batch.
Correct. Both are non-blocking and latency-tolerant — exactly the batch sweet spot.
Both pre-merge and CI lint typically block a developer; sync is required.
Sync HTTP and real-time fraud detection are both blocking; neither fits batch.

question: An engineer asks: 'Can I just look up which response goes with which input by their order in the response file?' What's the correct answer?
options: No — response order isn't guaranteed. Use the `custom_id` field on each response to correlate to the original request.
Yes — responses are returned in submission order by default.
Yes, but only if you submit fewer than 1,000 requests per batch.
No — you must wait for the batch to fully complete before reading any response.
explanations: Correct. Order isn't guaranteed; correlation must be done by `custom_id`.
There's no documented order guarantee; positional matching silently misaligns.
There's no documented small-batch ordering exception.
Whether you wait for completion is unrelated to ordering — even after completion, order isn't guaranteed.

question: A new SLA requires results within 12 hours of submission. You're on the Message Batches API. What does the math say about whether this is feasible?
options: Feasible if you submit every 6 hours.
Not feasible with batches alone — the 24h upper bound on processing exceeds the 12h SLA before any queue time is added.
Feasible if you set `priority: high` on each request.
Feasible if you cap each batch at 1,000 requests.
explanations: Submission cadence can't shrink the 24h processing upper bound; the SLA itself exceeds it.
Correct. Batch processing alone can take up to 24h; that's already double the 12h SLA. SLAs tighter than 24h require sync (or a hybrid with sync for SLA-bound traffic).
There is no documented priority field that bypasses the 24h upper bound.
Smaller batches don't change the per-batch processing upper bound.

question: Why is 'batch with sync fallback if a batch runs longer than expected' usually a bad design?
options: Sync and batch results aren't comparable, so the fallback returns inconsistent answers.
It violates Anthropic's terms of service.
You pay for the abandoned batch slot AND the sync re-run, and the worst case is no better than running plain sync from the start.
Sync API requests can't accept the same prompt format as batched ones.
explanations: Results from the same prompt are comparable across both APIs; that's not the issue.
There's no ToS prohibition on this pattern; it's just an anti-pattern.
Correct. Cost goes up (paid for both modes) and worst-case latency doesn't improve over plain sync. Choose one mode based on workload.
Prompt formats are the same; both APIs use Messages.

question: A developer batches a workload that previously used a synchronous tool-use loop with 3 tool calls per request. Each batched response now contains a single `tool_use` block with no follow-up. What is most likely happening?
options: The `tool_use` blocks need to be parsed differently in batch responses than in sync.
The model has been silently downgraded to a tool-incapable variant.
The batched response is corrupted and should be discarded.
The Batches API doesn't orchestrate multi-turn tool-use; it returns the first tool request and stops, because there's no harness to run tools mid-batch.
explanations: Block parsing is the same across APIs; the issue is missing orchestration, not formatting.
The model isn't silently swapped; the limitation is that batches don't orchestrate tool loops.
The response isn't corrupted — it's the documented behaviour for tool calls in batches.
Correct. Batches don't run tool loops mid-request — they emit the first tool_use and stop. The remediation is to keep the loop on sync (or pre-fetch and batch only the synthesis turn).

question: Which best describes how to use a small sample run before submitting a large batch?
options: Run 10–100 representative items synchronously, measure first-pass success against the validation rule (schema, classification), refine the prompt until success is high, then submit the full batch.
Submit 10 items as a small batch; iterate until they all pass; then scale.
Skip sampling — the model is deterministic on temperature 0.
Sample only after the first batch fails, to triage which prompts to fix.
explanations: Correct. Sync sampling exposes prompt issues in minutes; full-batch debugging costs 24h per cycle.
Even a small batch costs a 24h cycle to iterate; sync sampling is dramatically faster.
Determinism doesn't fix instruction ambiguity; it just makes the wrong interpretation consistent.
Sampling after failure means you've already paid the 24h cost — sample first.

question: An overnight document classification batch finishes in 2 hours on most nights. The dashboard team plans for 'results by 4am.' What's the architectural risk?
options: Anthropic charges more when batches finish faster than expected.
The 24h upper bound can hit any night with no warning; planning to typical-case latency means the dashboard occasionally has stale data.
The Batches API caches results for only 1 hour, so 2-hour completions risk losing data.
Batches finishing under 6h are automatically retried.
explanations: Pricing doesn't penalise fast completions; it's flat ~50% of sync.
Correct. Plan to the upper bound, not the typical case; 'usually fast' isn't a guarantee.
There's no documented 1-hour expiry; the issue is delivery time, not result retention.
There's no auto-retry policy based on completion time.

question: A team plans to 'batch all of our Claude calls' to capture the 50% cost saving across the platform. Which call site, if migrated, will most clearly break behaviour?
options: The weekly KPI report rendered into a dashboard on Monday morning.
The nightly anomaly-detection summary emailed at 7am.
The interactive chat UI where users type a question and wait for a response.
The monthly cost-allocation classifier triggered by a cron job.
explanations: Weekly KPI reports are non-blocking; batch fits.
Nightly summaries are non-blocking; batch fits.
Correct. Live chat is blocking; up-to-24h responses make the UX unusable.
Monthly cron-driven jobs are non-blocking; batch fits.

question: An engineer suggests using `custom_id` only when batches occasionally have failures, and skipping it for 'clean' workloads. What's the issue?
options: Anthropic charges extra to batches without `custom_id`.
Nothing — `custom_id` is only for failure tracking.
The batch will reject submissions over 1,000 requests if `custom_id` is missing.
Without `custom_id` you can't reliably correlate any response to its input — the response file isn't guaranteed to preserve submission order.
explanations: Pricing is flat; no fee for missing `custom_id`.
Correlation is the primary use, not just failure tracking.
There's no documented 1,000-request gate tied to `custom_id`.
Correct. `custom_id` is the only reliable correlation mechanism; without it, even a fully successful batch's responses can't be safely matched to inputs.

question: Which of the following is NOT a valid use case for the Message Batches API?
options: A real-time PR review bot that comments on opened pull requests.
A nightly dataset-labeling job over 500k examples.
A weekly compliance audit run on Sunday evening.
An eval run executed once per release.
explanations: Correct. PR review bots are tied to the developer's workflow — they need fast, blocking responses; batch is wrong here.
Nightly labeling is non-blocking; batch is a great fit.
Weekly audits are non-blocking; batch is a great fit.
Per-release evals are non-blocking; batch is a great fit.

question: An overnight extraction batch is submitted at 22:00 and the dashboard refreshes at 08:00 the next day. The team observes that on most nights, the batch finishes by 02:00 — but last Thursday it finished at 21:30 the next evening, missing the 08:00 dashboard refresh. What's the right interpretation?
options: Anthropic violated their SLA; the team should request a credit.
This is consistent with the documented behaviour: up to 24 hours, no SLA. Plan to the worst case (submit earlier or accept later refresh).
The batch was internally retried because of a transient model error.
The batch finishing later than usual indicates the prompt has a bug.
explanations: There is no SLA on the Batches API, so no SLA was violated and no credit applies.
Correct. The 24h upper bound can be hit on any given night; production design must hold at the worst case, not the median.
There's no documented user-visible internal retry; the more likely cause is normal variation within the 24h window.
Slow completion is a latency phenomenon; prompt bugs surface as failed responses, not slow ones.

question: A team needs to extract structured data from PDFs. The pipeline currently calls a `lookup_company_metadata` tool for each PDF as part of a multi-turn loop with Claude. They want to batch this for 50% savings. Which decomposition makes batching feasible while preserving the model's access to the metadata?
options: Run `lookup_company_metadata` deterministically in code before submission, embed the result in each batched request's prompt, and use a single-turn batched extraction.
Submit a batch where each request includes the `lookup_company_metadata` tool definition; the batch runtime will resolve the tool calls.
Send one batch with the lookup, then a second batch with the extraction, correlated by `custom_id`.
Use a hybrid 'batch with sync fallback' so the tool loop runs sync if needed.
explanations: Correct. Pre-fetch the metadata deterministically, then batch a single-turn synthesis — no tool loop required at submission time.
Batches don't orchestrate tool calls mid-request; the loop never advances.

Two-batch correlation via `custom_id` works for some pipelines but doesn't help if the lookup result depends on Claude's reasoning — and even when it does work, the lookup itself doesn't need a model and shouldn't go through Claude at all.
Hybrid sync fallback doubles cost and doesn't address the architectural mismatch.

question: An SRE asks: 'If we include the `tools` parameter in a batched request, will the model emit a `tool_use` block?' What's the most accurate answer?
options: No — `tools` is silently ignored in batched requests.
Yes — the model can emit a single `tool_use` block, but the batch runtime won't execute it; you'd need a sync follow-up to run the tool and continue the conversation.
Yes — and the batch runtime executes the tool transparently before returning the final answer.
Yes — and the batch runtime returns multiple turns of tool calls and results.
explanations: `tools` isn't ignored; the model can request a tool, but execution doesn't happen in batch.
Correct. `tools` works at the request-shape level — the model can emit one tool_use — but mid-request orchestration is absent, so multi-turn loops still need sync.
There is no transparent tool execution inside batches.
Multiple-turn orchestration isn't supported; you get at most a single `tool_use` per request.

question: A 30h SLA pipeline currently submits batches every 4 hours and meets the SLA worst case at 28h. Engineering proposes increasing the cadence to every 1 hour to 'have more headroom.' What's the trade-off?
options: Increasing cadence eliminates the 24h upper bound.
Cadence under 4h is forbidden by the API.
More batches mean more orchestration overhead and per-batch fixed costs but minimal SLA improvement — the 24h processing upper bound dominates the worst case regardless of cadence under ~6h.
Hourly cadence cuts processing time by 4x.
explanations: Cadence affects queue time, not processing time; the 24h upper bound stays the same.
There's no documented minimum cadence.
Correct. Worst-case end-to-end is `queue_wait + 24h`; cadence below the SLA buffer point gives diminishing returns because 24h dominates.
Per-batch processing time isn't reduced by submitting more often.

question: A team batches a 10,000-document classification job using `custom_id` values like 'doc-001' through 'doc-10000'. After the run, 12 responses come back with `custom_id` values they don't recognise (e.g., 'doc-99999'). What's the most likely explanation?
options: Failed responses receive a generic `custom_id` like 'doc-99999'.
Anthropic auto-generates `custom_id`s when collisions occur.
Batches occasionally inject test traffic that customers can ignore.
Their submission code has a bug — `custom_id`s are returned exactly as submitted; an unexpected value means it was sent that way.
explanations: Failed responses preserve the original `custom_id`; they don't get a generic one.
There's no auto-generation behaviour; the field is caller-supplied.
Batches don't inject test traffic into customer responses.
Correct. `custom_id` is caller-controlled and returned verbatim; unexpected values indicate a submission-side bug (off-by-one, log re-use, mis-keyed loop, etc.).

question: Which of the following best illustrates the cadence math for honoring a 36-hour SLA with batches whose processing takes up to 24 hours?
options: Submit at least every 12 hours so worst case is 12h queued + 24h processing = 36h.
Submit every 36 hours, matching the SLA exactly.
Submit every 24 hours.
Submit only after batches start failing.
explanations: Correct. SLA buffer = 36h − 24h = 12h; submit at least every 12h so the oldest queued item never exceeds the buffer.
36h cadence + 24h processing = 60h worst case, far past the SLA.
24h cadence + 24h processing = 48h worst case, still 12h over the SLA.
Cadence isn't event-triggered by failures; it must be planned proactively.

question: A legacy nightly job uses the synchronous API at full price. Migrating to batches yields ~50% savings, but the team also wants to know if they should keep the sync path 'just in case' as a primary route on busy nights. What's the right framing?
options: Always keep both paths in production for resilience.
Pick one mode based on whether the workload is blocking. The 'maybe sync, maybe batch' design doubles infrastructure complexity and erases most of the savings.
Batch is unreliable; sync should always be the default with batch as backup.
Use batch on weekdays, sync on weekends.
explanations: Dual paths add infra complexity; the workload is non-blocking, so sync isn't needed.
Correct. The migration should be decisive — non-blocking workload goes to batch; sync goes elsewhere. Hybridising the same workload across both modes adds cost and complexity.
Batch isn't unreliable — it has a different latency profile, which is fine for non-blocking work.
Day-of-week heuristics don't reflect any documented latency variation; pick by workload, not calendar.

question: A senior engineer claims: 'The Batches API guarantees delivery within 24 hours, so we can promise customers a 25-hour SLA.' Which response is correct?
options: The 24h figure is actually the median, so the worst case is unbounded — a 25h customer SLA is far too tight.
Correct — the upper bound effectively functions as an SLA.
The 24h figure is an upper bound but Anthropic publishes no SLA — there's no guarantee, only a worst-case window. A customer SLA built on it would be promising what Anthropic doesn't.
The 24h figure only applies to single-region deployments; multi-region has its own SLA.
explanations: 24h is the documented upper bound, not the median; this misstates the figure.
Upper bounds without SLAs aren't enforceable — Anthropic doesn't owe credits for slippage.
Correct. 'Up to 24 hours' is a documented characteristic, not a contractual SLA; customer-facing SLAs need a buffer or a sync component.
There's no documented region-specific SLA structure for batches.

question: Which sequence is the most resilient design for a vendor running structured-extraction batches under a 30h customer SLA?
options: Sync everything to avoid batch's lack of SLA, even at 2x cost.
Single daily batch at 02:00 UTC → email customers if a batch slips → resubmit the entire batch on any failure.
Batch every request initially → fall back to sync per request if a batch runs over 6 hours.
Sync sample for prompt validation → 4h cadence batches with `custom_id` → targeted resubmission of only failed `custom_id`s → keep blocking workflows (e.g., CI lint) on sync.
explanations: All-sync defeats the 50% savings on the bulk workload that's perfectly suited to batches.
Daily cadence breaks the 30h SLA worst case; whole-batch resubmission wastes a 24h cycle on partial failures.
Batch+sync fallback doubles cost (you pay for the abandoned slot) and doesn't beat plain sync's worst case.
Correct. Pre-batch refinement maximises first-pass success, 4h cadence honours the 30h SLA worst case, `custom_id` enables targeted resubmission, and sync stays where blocking demands it.

question: A team submits 50,000 batched extractions, all using `custom_id` values that are valid but happen to be reused from a previous run (e.g., 'invoice-1' to 'invoice-50000' overlapping with last week's IDs). What's the operational risk?
options: If the team merges this run's responses into the same store keyed only by `custom_id`, this run's results will silently overwrite or conflict with last week's. `custom_id` should be unique within the namespace your pipeline uses to look results up.
Anthropic rejects batches whose `custom_id`s collide with prior batches.
The Batches API auto-namespaces `custom_id`s by batch ID, so reuse is safe.
Reusing `custom_id`s halves the cost saving for the second batch.
explanations: Correct. `custom_id` is opaque to Anthropic — reuse is fine API-side, but downstream stores keyed on `custom_id` alone will collide. Either include the batch ID/date in the key or use globally unique identifiers.
